nodes.title: Physical and Chemical Foundations
nodes.essence: A patient is a physical object.

nodes.title: Physics of the Body
nodes.essence: The body is matter, and it obeys the same laws as a steam engine, a river or a loudspeaker. This area answers: which physical laws constrain what a living body can be and do, and what do they predict about how it is built and how it fails?

nodes.title: Energy and Thermodynamics
nodes.essence: A living body is an open system held far from equilibrium. It takes in chemical energy as food and oxygen, uses a fraction to build and maintain order (gradients, macromolecules, movement) and releases the rest as heat and low-grade waste.

nodes.title: Fluids, Pressure and Flow
nodes.essence: Blood, air, urine, lymph and cerebrospinal fluid all move because something pushes them down a pressure gradient against a resistance.

nodes.title: Diffusion, Osmosis and Transport
nodes.essence: Molecules move at random, and random motion carries more of them from where they are concentrated to where they are not. This is diffusion, and it needs no energy, no pump and no intention; it is the second law acting on matter.

nodes.title: Electricity and Excitable Membranes
nodes.essence: The body's electricity is not electrons in wires but ions in water, separated by a membrane that is a few nanometres thick and almost impermeable.

nodes.title: Mechanics and Materials
nodes.essence: The body is a structure that must stand, move, pump and stretch for decades without failing, and it is built from materials with peculiar properties: soft, wet, fibrous, self-repairing and alive.

nodes.title: Waves, Sound, Light and Radiation
nodes.essence: Almost everything medicine knows about the inside of a living body without cutting it open comes from waves: sound reflected from tissue boundaries, X-rays attenuated by bone, radio waves emitted by hydrogen nuclei in a magnetic field, gamma rays from a tracer, and light absorbed by haemoglobin.

nodes.title: Scale and Allometry
nodes.essence: Size is not neutral.

nodes.title: Chemistry of Life
nodes.essence: Physics sets the forces; chemistry supplies the molecules those forces act on. This area answers: what chemical facts must be true for a body to exist, stay within the narrow conditions that keep it alive, extract energy from food, and pass signals between molecules?

nodes.title: Atoms, Bonds and Molecular Shape
nodes.essence: Living matter is made of about a dozen elements, dominated by carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, held together by a small repertoire of bonds whose strengths span three orders of magnitude.

nodes.title: Water, Solutions and Concentration
nodes.essence: The body is about 60% water by mass, and almost every reaction in it happens in solution.

nodes.title: Acids, Bases and Buffers
nodes.essence: The hydrogen ion concentration of blood is held at about 40 nanomoles per litre (pH 7.40), a million times lower than that of sodium, and normally within about ±5 nmol/L of that value; outside pH 6.8–7.8 enzymes misfold, membranes fail and the heart stops.

nodes.title: Redox and Electron Transfer
nodes.essence: The body runs on a slow, controlled combustion.

nodes.title: Kinetics, Equilibrium and Catalysis
nodes.essence: Thermodynamics says which way a reaction can go; kinetics says how fast it gets there, and in the body the two are deliberately separated.

nodes.title: Carbon Chemistry and Molecular Recognition
nodes.essence: Life is carbon chemistry because carbon alone forms four strong bonds to itself and to other atoms, in chains, branches and rings, making an effectively unlimited set of stable shapes.

nodes.title: Quantitative and Scientific Foundations
nodes.essence: Medicine is a quantitative science before it is a clinical one.

nodes.title: Probability and Measurement
nodes.essence: Medicine acts on numbers it cannot trust completely: a blood pressure that varies by the minute, a laboratory value with a 5% error, a test that misses one case in ten, a prevalence estimated from a sample.

nodes.title: Measurement Error and Biological Variation
nodes.essence: Every number in medicine is a measurement of a quantity that was already varying before the instrument touched it.

nodes.title: Probability
nodes.essence: Medicine never knows; it estimates.

nodes.title: Distributions and Descriptive Statistics
nodes.essence: A distribution is the shape that probability takes over the possible values of a quantity: how heights, blood pressures, survival times or counts of infections are spread across a population.

nodes.title: Bayesian Reasoning
nodes.essence: Diagnosis is the revision of belief by evidence, and Bayes' theorem is the arithmetic of that revision. Before any test, a clinician holds a probability that the patient has a disease (the prior, or pre-test probability), drawn from prevalence, the history and the examination.

nodes.title: Inference and Causation
nodes.essence: A study observes a few hundred patients; medicine wants a rule for millions. A drug appears to help; medicine wants to know whether it caused the help.

nodes.title: Hypothesis Testing and Confidence Intervals
nodes.essence: A study measures a sample, but medicine wants to know about everyone like the sample.

nodes.title: Regression, Adjustment and Survival Analysis
nodes.essence: Most medical questions involve many variables at once: does this drug lower mortality after allowing for the fact that the patients who received it were older and sicker? How much does each of smoking, blood pressure and cholesterol contribute to a person's ten-year risk?

nodes.title: Causal Inference
nodes.essence: Medicine's useful knowledge is causal: smoking causes lung cancer, this drug lowers mortality, that exposure is safe.

nodes.title: Systems and Models
nodes.essence: The body is a system: many parts, connected, exchanging substance and signal, holding itself steady and changing over time. This area answers: what general patterns does any such system show, independent of what it is made of, and how does one build and judge a model of it?

nodes.title: The Scientific Method and Models
nodes.essence: Medicine was practised for two thousand years on theories that were coherent, taught by authorities, confirmed by experience and wrong: bloodletting for fever, humours for everything.

nodes.title: Feedback and Control
nodes.essence: A body keeps its temperature, blood pressure, glucose, pH and a hundred other variables within narrow limits while the world outside and the demands inside change constantly.

nodes.title: Compartment Models and Exponential Processes
nodes.essence: A great deal of medicine is the bookkeeping of substances moving between pools: a drug from gut to blood to tissue to urine, oxygen from air to blood, a tracer through the kidney, people from susceptible to infected to recovered.

nodes.title: Nonlinear Dynamics, Oscillations and Networks
nodes.essence: Linear models, in which effects add and doubling the cause doubles the effect, describe the body well in small ranges and badly at the edges, where medicine does most of its work.

nodes.title: Information, Signals and Noise
nodes.essence: The body is run by messages: a hormone concentration, a train of nerve impulses, a sequence of bases, a cytokine gradient, and the clinician reads messages of her own, an electrocardiogram, an image, a history.

nodes.title: Biochemistry and Molecular Biology
nodes.essence: Biochemistry is chemistry organised into a living system: the same bonds, gradients, redox reactions and acid–base equilibria as in a flask, but arranged in polymers, pathways, codes and circuits that maintain themselves far from equilibrium.

nodes.title: Macromolecules
nodes.essence: A cell is built from four kinds of large molecule, and each kind is the answer to a different problem. Proteins solve the problem of doing things: with twenty chemically distinct side chains they fold into shapes that bind, catalyse, pump, pull and signal.

nodes.title: Proteins: structure and folding
nodes.essence: A protein is a chain of amino acids that folds into a specific three-dimensional shape, and the shape is the function. Twenty side chains of different size, charge and affinity for water give enough variety to build enzymes, pumps, receptors, motors, fibres and antibodies.

nodes.title: Enzymes and catalysis
nodes.essence: An enzyme is a protein (occasionally an Ribonucleic Acid (RNA)) that speeds up one reaction by binding its transition state more tightly than its substrate, lowering the activation barrier without touching the equilibrium.

nodes.title: Nucleic acids
nodes.essence: Deoxyribonucleic Acid (DNA) and Ribonucleic Acid (RNA) are polymers of four nucleotides whose order carries information and whose chemistry lets that information be copied, read and corrected.

nodes.title: Lipids and membranes
nodes.essence: Lipids are the molecules that water rejects, and that rejection is what makes cells possible.

nodes.title: Carbohydrates and glycobiology
nodes.essence: Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes and ketones, and their many hydroxyl groups give them three roles that look unrelated but share one chemistry. As fuel, glucose is the molecule every tissue can burn and the brain depends on.

nodes.title: Metabolism
nodes.essence: Metabolism is how a cell extracts free energy from food, converts one kind of molecule into another, and keeps both processes matched to demand.

nodes.title: Bioenergetics: ATP and redox carriers
nodes.essence: A living cell is an open system held far from equilibrium, and bioenergetics is the accounting of how it pays to stay there.

nodes.title: Glycolysis, TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation
nodes.essence: Glucose is oxidised to carbon dioxide in three stages: glycolysis in the cytosol splits it to two pyruvate, the Tricarboxylic Acid (TCA) cycle in the mitochondrial matrix strips the carbons to carbon dioxide and loads electrons onto Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide (NAD) and Flavin Adenine Dinucleotide (FAD), and the respiratory chain in the inner membrane passes those electrons to oxygen while pumping protons that drive Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP) synthase.

nodes.title: Lipid metabolism
nodes.essence: Fat is the body's long-term energy store, and lipid metabolism is the set of pathways that deposit it after a meal, mobilise it during fasting, burn it for Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP), and convert surplus carbohydrate into it.

nodes.title: Amino acid and nitrogen metabolism
nodes.essence: Amino acids are the only major fuel with nitrogen, and the body has no way to store either.

nodes.title: Metabolic integration and the fed–fasted cycle
nodes.essence: Meals are intermittent and the brain's demand for glucose is continuous, so the body must store fuel after eating and release it in the right form between meals.

nodes.title: Vitamins, minerals and cofactors
nodes.essence: A vitamin is a small molecule the body needs in milligram or microgram amounts because it cannot make it, and almost every one is needed because an enzyme uses it to do chemistry that amino-acid side chains cannot: carry electrons, stabilise a carbanion, move a one-carbon unit, activate an acyl group.

nodes.title: Nucleotide metabolism
nodes.essence: Nucleotides are the monomers of Deoxyribonucleic Acid (DNA) and Ribonucleic Acid (RNA), the energy currency (Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP)) and the core of the coenzymes; a dividing cell needs a large supply.

nodes.title: Genetic information flow
nodes.essence: This area follows information from a sequence of Deoxyribonucleic Acid (DNA) to a working protein in its right place, and back to the copy that is passed to the next cell.

nodes.title: DNA replication and repair
nodes.essence: Before a cell divides it must copy about 3 billion base pairs, and between divisions it must undo the tens of thousands of chemical lesions its Deoxyribonucleic Acid (DNA) suffers every day.

nodes.title: Transcription and RNA processing
nodes.essence: Transcription copies a gene into Ribonucleic Acid (RNA), a disposable working copy that can be made in whatever amount the cell needs and discarded when it is not.

nodes.title: Translation and protein targeting
nodes.essence: Translation converts a sequence of nucleotides into a sequence of amino acids using a code of three-letter words, read by transfer RNAs (tRNAs) that are charged by enzymes which are the true decoders, on a ribosome whose catalytic heart is Ribonucleic Acid (RNA).

nodes.title: Gene regulation and epigenetic mechanisms
nodes.essence: Every nucleated cell in a body carries the same genome, so what makes a neuron differ from a hepatocyte is which genes are read, how much, and when.

nodes.title: Molecular techniques
nodes.essence: The techniques of molecular biology are the cell's own enzymes and recognition rules taken out of the cell and used as tools.

nodes.title: Cell signalling
nodes.essence: A cell is sealed inside a membrane that nothing useful can cross on its own, yet it must take in fuel, hold an electrical charge, and respond to hormones, transmitters, growth factors and antigens arriving from outside.

nodes.title: Membrane transport and ion gradients
nodes.essence: A lipid bilayer lets almost nothing charged or polar through, so every ion, sugar and amino acid that enters or leaves a cell does so through a protein: a channel that opens a pore, a carrier that changes shape around its cargo, or a pump that spends Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP).

nodes.title: Receptors and ligands
nodes.essence: A receptor is a protein that binds a specific molecule and changes shape, and in that change a chemical message becomes a cellular response.

nodes.title: Second messengers and kinase cascades
nodes.essence: A receptor at the surface has changed shape; now the inside of the cell must hear about it.

nodes.title: Signal amplification, integration and termination
nodes.essence: A signalling pathway is not a wire; it is a small computer.

nodes.title: Cell Biology
nodes.essence: The cell is the smallest thing that is alive, and this layer is where the two roots of the tree meet in a living unit.

nodes.title: Cell structure
nodes.essence: This area asks how a cell is built so that chemistry, energy and information can work together in one unit. Biochemistry (layer 02) supplies the parts: enzymes, membranes, pumps, genes and signalling cascades. A cell is what happens when those parts are arranged in space.

nodes.title: Organelles and compartmentalization
nodes.essence: A eukaryotic cell is not a bag of enzymes but a set of membrane-bounded compartments, each with its own chemistry.

nodes.title: The cytoskeleton and cell motility
nodes.essence: The cytoskeleton is the cell's bones, muscles and railways in one system of protein polymers: actin filaments, microtubules and intermediate filaments.

nodes.title: Membrane trafficking and secretion
nodes.essence: Cells move proteins and lipids between compartments and across the plasma membrane without ever letting them cross a bilayer: they pinch off a vesicle from one membrane and fuse it with another.

nodes.title: Protein quality control and degradation
nodes.essence: A cell makes millions of protein molecules an hour, and many misfold, are damaged by heat or oxidation, or are no longer needed.

nodes.title: The cell life cycle
nodes.essence: A tissue is a population of cells, and its size and composition are set by four decisions that each cell makes: divide, differentiate, stop permanently, or die. This area describes the machinery of each decision and how they are coupled.

nodes.title: The cell cycle and its checkpoints
nodes.essence: The cell cycle is the ordered sequence by which one cell becomes two: grow (G1), copy the genome exactly once (S), check and prepare (G2), divide (M).

nodes.title: Mitosis, meiosis and chromosome segregation
nodes.essence: Two metres of Deoxyribonucleic Acid (DNA) in 46 chromosomes must be shared exactly between two daughters at every one of the ~10^16 divisions of a human lifetime.

nodes.title: Cell death: apoptosis, necrosis and autophagy
nodes.essence: Cells die in two fundamentally different ways. Apoptosis is a programme: the cell dismantles itself with dedicated proteases, packages its contents and is eaten by neighbours without spilling or inflammation.

nodes.title: Senescence and telomeres
nodes.essence: A normal human cell in culture divides a limited number of times (the Hayflick limit, ~50 doublings for fetal fibroblasts) and then stops permanently while staying alive: it is senescent.

nodes.title: Stem cells, differentiation and regeneration
nodes.essence: Every cell carries the same genome, yet a neuron, a hepatocyte and a red cell could not be more different.

nodes.title: Cells in community
nodes.essence: A human is ~3 × 10^13 cells that must act as one organism. This area asks what a cell needs in order to live among others: something to hold on to, a way to talk to its neighbours and to distant tissues, and a way to cope when its environment turns hostile.

nodes.title: Cell adhesion and the extracellular matrix
nodes.essence: Cells become a tissue by sticking to each other and to a scaffold they secrete. The Extracellular Matrix (ECM) is that scaffold: collagen for tensile strength, elastin for recoil, proteoglycans that hold water and resist compression, and adhesive glycoproteins that cells grip.

nodes.title: Cell-to-cell communication and junctions
nodes.essence: A multicellular body works only if cells agree on what to do.

nodes.title: The cellular stress response
nodes.essence: Every cell lives in conditions that vary: oxygen falls, temperature rises, nutrients run out, toxins and radiation damage molecules, pathogens invade.

nodes.title: Genetics, Evolution and Development
nodes.essence: Layer 03 described a cell with a repertoire. This layer explains how an organism made of such cells comes to be the way it is, from three directions.

nodes.title: Inheritance
nodes.essence: This area answers the question a patient asks when a relative falls ill: will it happen to me, and to my children?

nodes.title: Mendelian inheritance and pedigrees
nodes.essence: Mendel's insight (1866) was that heredity is particulate: each parent passes one of two copies of each factor, the copies do not blend, and which copy is passed is chance.
keyTerms: Haploinsufficiency, dominant negative, gain of function

nodes.title: Chromosomes and cytogenetics
nodes.essence: The human genome is packaged into 46 chromosomes, 22 autosomal pairs and two sex chromosomes, ~3.1 billion base pairs in all, each chromosome a single Deoxyribonucleic Acid (DNA) molecule wound around histones.

nodes.title: Genomic variation and mutation
nodes.essence: Any two unrelated human genomes differ at roughly 4–5 million positions, and every person carries ~60–100 new mutations that neither parent had.
keyTerms: Loss of function / gain of function

nodes.title: Complex traits and heritability
nodes.essence: Height, blood pressure, body mass and the risk of diabetes, coronary disease, schizophrenia and most cancers all run in families, yet none follows a Mendelian pattern.

nodes.title: Epigenetic inheritance and imprinting
nodes.essence: The Deoxyribonucleic Acid (DNA) sequence is not the only heritable information in a cell. Methyl groups on cytosine and marks on histones decide which genes are open, and are copied through cell division, so a liver cell's daughters are liver cells.

nodes.title: Mitochondrial genetics
nodes.essence: Every cell carries a second genome. Mitochondrial Deoxyribonucleic Acid (mtDNA) is a circle of ~16.6 kilobases with 37 genes, present in hundreds to thousands of copies per cell and inherited only from the egg.

nodes.title: Evolution
nodes.essence: Inheritance explains how a genome passes from parent to child; evolution explains why the genome is what it is. This area asks the question that the rest of medicine rarely asks aloud: why is the body vulnerable in the particular ways it is?

nodes.title: Natural selection and population genetics
nodes.essence: Evolution is a change in the frequency of alleles in a population over generations. It needs only variation (mutation), inheritance (meiosis and Mendel) and differential reproduction.

nodes.title: Evolutionary medicine
nodes.essence: Most of medicine asks how a disease happens. Evolutionary medicine asks why the body is built so that it can fail that way. Selection does not produce health; it produces reproductive success in past environments, with whatever variation and history it has.

nodes.title: Host–pathogen coevolution and resistance
nodes.essence: Hosts and pathogens evolve in response to each other, and the contest is unequal in tempo: a bacterium's generation is minutes, a human's decades.

nodes.title: Human evolution and variation
nodes.essence: Modern humans arose in Africa within the last ~300,000 years, left it in small numbers ~60,000–70,000 years ago and spread across the planet, picking up a few percent of archaic ancestry on the way.

nodes.title: Development
nodes.essence: This area answers how one cell becomes a body, and how that body then grows, matures and declines.

nodes.title: Fertilization and early embryogenesis
nodes.essence: A human begins as one cell formed when a sperm fuses with an egg; in two weeks that cell becomes a hollow ball, implants, separates placenta from body, and lays down the first axis.

nodes.title: Germ layers and organogenesis
nodes.essence: In the third week the two-layered disc rearranges into three layers by gastrulation, and in the following five weeks those layers fold, bud, migrate and hollow into every organ.

nodes.title: Morphogens, patterning and developmental genes
nodes.essence: How does a cell in an embryo know where it is? A handful of secreted signalling molecules form concentration gradients across fields of cells, and cells read their position from the local concentration, switching on different transcription factors at different thresholds.

nodes.title: Congenital malformations and teratogens
nodes.essence: About 3% of live-born infants have a major structural abnormality, a leading cause of infant death in high-income countries. Causes are chromosomal (~10%), single-gene (~10–15%), teratogenic (~5–10%), and in roughly half of cases unknown or multifactorial.

nodes.title: Growth, puberty and aging
nodes.essence: Development does not end at birth.

nodes.title: Sex determination and differentiation
nodes.essence: Every embryo begins with the same bipotential gonad, two sets of ducts and one set of external folds. A single gene on the Y chromosome tips the gonad toward testis; the testis then makes two hormones, and those hormones, not the chromosomes, build the rest of the male body.

nodes.title: Tissues and Anatomy
nodes.essence: This layer is the body as a built thing: the four tissues it is made of, the rules by which they are packaged, supplied, wired and loaded, and the particular arrangement of them in each region.

nodes.title: Tissues
nodes.essence: Between the cell and the organ lies the tissue: a population of cells and the matrix they secrete, organised so that the whole does something no single cell can.

nodes.title: Epithelium
nodes.essence: An epithelium is a sheet of cells, sealed to one another and standing on a basement membrane, that separates two compartments and controls what passes between them.

nodes.title: Connective tissue, bone and cartilage
nodes.essence: Connective tissue is the tissue in which the cells are few and the product between them does the work.

nodes.title: Muscle tissue
nodes.essence: Muscle turns the chemical energy of Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP) into force by letting myosin heads pull on actin filaments.

nodes.title: Nervous tissue
nodes.essence: Nervous tissue is built to carry information fast and far, and every structural feature follows from that demand.

nodes.title: Blood and haematopoiesis
nodes.essence: Blood is a connective tissue whose matrix is liquid, which lets it be pumped through every other tissue carrying oxygen, fuel, heat, hormones, waste and the cells of defence and repair. An adult has about 5 L, roughly 7% of body mass: a little under half cells, the rest plasma.

nodes.title: Body organization
nodes.essence: Between the tissues and the regions lies a set of organising principles that hold for the whole body: a coordinate system for describing it, a scheme of closed compartments that packages it, a vascular tree and lymphatic drain that supply and clear every part of it, a segmental wiring diagram inherited from the embryo, and a mechanical design of levers and bearings.

nodes.title: Anatomical language, planes and regions
nodes.essence: Anatomy needs a coordinate system before it can say anything, because "above", "in front of" and "left" change meaning as soon as a patient lies down or is viewed on a screen.

nodes.title: Body cavities, fascia and compartments
nodes.essence: The body is not one bag but a nested set of compartments: the skull, the spinal canal, the thorax with its two pleural sacs and pericardium, the abdomen and pelvis with the peritoneal sac, and in every limb a set of osteofascial compartments.

nodes.title: Vascular and lymphatic architecture
nodes.essence: The circulation is a closed loop of two pumps and two circuits in series, with the systemic organs in parallel between aorta and venae cavae.

nodes.title: Segmental innervation, dermatomes and referred pain
nodes.essence: The body is built in segments, and the nervous system keeps the plan long after the body has hidden it.

nodes.title: Biomechanics of the musculoskeletal system
nodes.essence: The skeleton is a set of levers, the joints their bearings, and the muscles motors attached close to the pivots. That trades force for speed and range: the muscles and joints that move a hand carry several times the load in it.

nodes.title: Regional anatomy
nodes.essence: Regional anatomy is the body described place by place: what lies next to what, and therefore what is injured, compressed, infected or operated on together. An atlas does this exhaustively.

nodes.title: Head, neck and spine
nodes.essence: The head, neck and spine hold the central nervous system in a rigid case and route everything that enters or leaves it, with the airway, gullet and great vessels, through a space a few centimetres wide. Three facts explain most of the region's medicine.

nodes.title: Thorax
nodes.essence: The thorax is a bellows with a pump inside it.

nodes.title: Abdomen and pelvis
nodes.essence: The abdomen and pelvis hold the gut, its glands, the kidneys and the reproductive organs inside one peritoneal sac and a muscular wall that must be both strong and openable.

nodes.title: Upper and lower limbs
nodes.essence: The two limbs are built on one plan (a girdle, one proximal bone, two distal bones, then a hand or foot) tuned to opposite ends of a trade-off: the upper limb for reach and grip, the lower for carrying the body.

nodes.title: Physiology
nodes.essence: Physiology is the account of how a body of some 37 trillion cells, each needing oxygen, fuel and a narrow range of temperature, pH and ionic composition, keeps every one of them alive while the whole organism runs, fasts, sleeps or fights an infection.

nodes.title: Integrative principles
nodes.essence: Before any organ system can be understood, the reader needs to know what the organ systems are for: which whole-body quantities they defend, how tightly, with what reserves, and what happens when the whole body is pushed, by exertion, heat, cold, injury or the clock.

nodes.title: Homeostasis and set points
nodes.essence: Homeostasis is the maintenance of the internal environment within limits that cells can tolerate, by negative feedback: a sensor measures a variable, a comparator holds it against a set point, and an effector acts to shrink the difference.

nodes.title: Body fluid compartments and electrolytes
nodes.essence: About 60% of an adult's mass is water, divided by two barriers into three compartments: the cell membrane separates intracellular from extracellular fluid, and the capillary wall splits the extracellular fluid into interstitium and plasma.

nodes.title: Acid–base physiology
nodes.essence: Extracellular hydrogen ion concentration is held at ~40 nmol/L (pH 7.40, range 7.35–7.45), a millionth of the sodium concentration, because proteins change shape with small shifts in pH.

nodes.title: Thermoregulation and energy balance
nodes.essence: The body is a heat engine that converts chemical energy from food into work, storage and, mostly, heat, and it holds its core at ~37 °C whether the air is 0 °C or 40 °C.

nodes.title: Exercise and stress physiology
nodes.essence: Exercise raises oxygen consumption from ~250 mL/min at rest to 3–5 L/min, an increase no single organ can supply alone: the heart pumps four to five times more, ventilation rises twentyfold, blood is redirected from gut and kidney to muscle, and muscle extracts three times more oxygen per litre.

nodes.title: Sleep and circadian rhythms
nodes.essence: The body keeps time.

nodes.title: Nervous system
nodes.essence: The nervous system is the body's fast signalling and control layer: it senses the world and the body, decides, and acts through muscle and gland within milliseconds to seconds, where hormones take minutes to hours.

nodes.title: Membrane potential and the action potential
nodes.essence: Every cell holds a voltage across its membrane because ions are unequally distributed and the membrane is selectively permeable; a nerve or muscle cell can additionally fire an action potential, a stereotyped, self-propagating reversal of that voltage that carries information without decrement over a metre of axon.

nodes.title: Synaptic transmission and neurotransmitters
nodes.essence: An action potential cannot jump between cells, so at the synapse it is converted into a chemical signal: calcium enters the terminal, vesicles release transmitter into a 20 nm cleft, and receptors on the next cell turn the transmitter back into current or into a slower biochemical change.

nodes.title: Sensory systems
nodes.essence: A sensory system converts one form of physical energy (pressure, stretch, temperature, photons, sound, chemicals) into a receptor potential, encodes its intensity as spike frequency and its quality as which fibre is firing, relays it through a small number of synapses to the thalamus and cortex, and sharpens it at every stage by inhibition and adaptation.

nodes.title: Motor control
nodes.essence: Movement is produced by one final common path, the alpha motor neuron and the muscle fibres it owns, and everything else in the motor system decides when, how strongly and in what pattern those neurons fire.
keyTerms: Upper vs lower motor neuron signs

nodes.title: The autonomic nervous system
nodes.essence: The autonomic nervous system is the motor system of the viscera: it runs the heart, vessels, airways, gut, bladder, pupils, glands and metabolism without conscious command, and it is the fast effector of nearly every homeostatic loop.

nodes.title: Higher functions: memory, language and consciousness
nodes.essence: The cerebral cortex, some 16 billion neurons in a sheet a few millimetres thick, adds to the reflexes and maps below it the capacities that define a person: storing experience, manipulating symbols, directing attention, and being awake and aware.

nodes.title: Pain
nodes.essence: Pain is a sensory system with a threat detector at the periphery and a volume control at every relay.

nodes.title: Cardiovascular system
nodes.essence: The circulation exists because diffusion works only over micrometres. Every cell in a 70 kg body must sit within a few tens of micrometres of a capillary, and the capillaries must be fed by a pressure head high enough to drive blood through them and bring it back.

nodes.title: The cardiac cycle and pump function
nodes.essence: The heart is two pumps in series, each filling at low pressure and ejecting at high pressure through valves moved only by pressure differences.

nodes.title: Cardiac electrophysiology
nodes.essence: The heart times itself.

nodes.title: Hemodynamics and blood pressure regulation
nodes.essence: Blood flows from aorta to right atrium because the heart creates a pressure difference of ~95 mmHg across a resistance set almost entirely by the arterioles.

nodes.title: Microcirculation and capillary exchange
nodes.essence: The circulation exists to deliver blood to some ten billion capillaries, each a tube of single endothelial cells 5–10 µm wide, together presenting a few hundred square metres of wall to the tissues.

nodes.title: The lymphatic system
nodes.essence: The blood circulation is a closed loop with a leak: every day a few litres of plasma water and about 100 g of protein filter out of the capillaries into the interstitium and do not come back the way they left. The lymphatic system is the return path.

nodes.title: Respiratory system
nodes.essence: The lung brings ~4 L/min of fresh air and ~5 L/min of venous blood within a third of a micrometre of each other across ~70 m² of membrane, so that oxygen and carbon dioxide can move by diffusion alone, and it does this with a pump that costs ~3% of resting energy and is driven by the chemistry of the blood it serves.

nodes.title: Ventilation and lung mechanics
nodes.essence: Air moves into the lung because the respiratory muscles enlarge the thorax, pleural pressure falls, the alveoli expand and their pressure drops a centimetre of water below atmospheric; expiration at rest is the stretched lung recoiling.

nodes.title: Gas exchange and transport
nodes.essence: Oxygen moves from air to mitochondrion down a staircase of partial pressures, and carbon dioxide climbs it in reverse; the lung keeps the top of the staircase high and the carriers in the blood do the rest.

nodes.title: Ventilation–perfusion matching
nodes.essence: Arterial blood gases are decided not by how much air and blood the lung receives but by how well they are matched, alveolus by alveolus.

nodes.title: Control of breathing
nodes.essence: Breathing is the output of a feedback loop that holds arterial carbon dioxide within about ±3 mmHg of 40 across a twentyfold range of metabolic demand, and falls back on oxygen as an emergency signal below ~60 mmHg.

nodes.title: The pulmonary circulation
nodes.essence: The lung is the only organ that receives the whole cardiac output, and it does so at a sixth of the systemic pressure.

nodes.title: Renal system
nodes.essence: The kidney answers one question continuously: given what the body has eaten, made and lost today, what must leave in the urine so that the volume and composition of the extracellular fluid stay constant?

nodes.title: Glomerular filtration and clearance
nodes.essence: The kidney cleans the blood by a wasteful-looking strategy: it filters a fifth of the plasma that passes through it, about 180 L a day, into a tubule, then reabsorbs 99% of the water and almost all the solute it wants to keep.

nodes.title: Tubular transport and the countercurrent system
nodes.essence: The tubule turns 180 L of protein-free plasma a day into 1–2 L of urine whose composition is exactly what the body needs to lose.

nodes.title: Sodium, water and volume regulation
nodes.essence: The body regulates two different quantities with two different loops that are easy to confuse. Osmolality (how concentrated the body fluids are) is sensed by hypothalamic osmoreceptors and corrected by water: thirst and Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH).

nodes.title: Potassium, calcium, phosphate and renal acid–base
nodes.essence: Beyond sodium and water, the kidney is the final arbiter of four quantities whose plasma concentrations must stay within narrow bands because excitable cells and the skeleton depend on them: potassium, calcium, phosphate and hydrogen ion.

nodes.title: Gastrointestinal system
nodes.essence: The gastrointestinal system takes irregular, bulky, chemically diverse and microbially contaminated input and converts it into a steady, sterile supply of small molecules for the blood.

nodes.title: Motility and its neural control
nodes.essence: The gut is a muscular tube about nine metres long that must move food forward at the pace digestion and absorption can handle, mix it with secretions, hold it when storage is needed and expel what is left. It does this with its own nervous system.

nodes.title: Secretion, digestion and absorption
nodes.essence: Food is polymer: starch, protein, triglyceride.

nodes.title: The liver as metabolic hub
nodes.essence: Everything absorbed from the gut (except fat in chylomicrons) passes through the liver before it reaches the rest of the body, and the liver decides what the body sees.

nodes.title: The gut barrier and microbiome
nodes.essence: The gut lumen is outside the body. Its ~30 m² of epithelium separates the sterile interior from a dense community of microbes, roughly 10¹³ bacterial cells in the colon alone, at densities of 10¹¹–10¹² per gram of content, together with the food antigens of every meal.

nodes.title: Endocrine system
nodes.essence: The nervous system sends private messages down wires; the endocrine system broadcasts chemical messages in the blood and relies on receptors to decide who listens.

nodes.title: Hormone classes, axes and feedback
nodes.essence: A hormone is a chemical released into the blood by one tissue to change the behaviour of distant tissues that carry its receptor.

nodes.title: Glucose homeostasis
nodes.essence: The brain burns ~120 g of glucose a day, cannot store it and cannot use fatty acids, so plasma glucose must stay between roughly 4 and 8 mmol/L whether the body has just eaten 100 g of carbohydrate or has fasted for two days.

nodes.title: Thyroid, adrenal and stress hormones
nodes.essence: Two glands set the body's tempo. The thyroid sets the baseline metabolic rate of nearly every cell over weeks, through a hormone whose supply is buffered so heavily that output barely changes from day to day.

nodes.title: Calcium and bone mineral metabolism
nodes.essence: Ionised calcium in extracellular fluid (~1.2 mmol/L) must be held within a few percent because it sets the threshold of every excitable membrane, triggers every muscle contraction and secretion, and is a ubiquitous second messenger.

nodes.title: Reproductive endocrinology
nodes.essence: Reproduction is run by one axis in both sexes: hypothalamic Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH), pituitary Luteinising Hormone (LH) and Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH), and gonadal steroids made from cholesterol. The axis is unusual in three ways.

nodes.title: Blood
nodes.essence: Blood is the one tissue that is a fluid, ~5 L of it in an adult, and the physiology of blood is the physiology of what that fluid must carry and how it must behave.

nodes.title: Red cells, haemoglobin and iron
nodes.essence: Oxygen is poorly soluble in water (~3 mL per litre of plasma at arterial tension), so the body packs ~150 g/L of haemoglobin into cells that carry ~200 mL of oxygen per litre of blood, seventy times more.

nodes.title: Haemostasis and coagulation
nodes.essence: Blood must stay liquid inside vessels and solidify within minutes at a hole, and nowhere else.

nodes.title: Blood groups and transfusion compatibility
nodes.essence: Red cells carry hundreds of inherited surface molecules, and a transfusion is a transplant of tissue the recipient's immune system may recognise as foreign. Two systems matter above all the others.
keyTerms: Haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn

nodes.title: Reproduction and the life course
nodes.essence: Every other area of physiology describes one body holding itself steady.

nodes.title: Gametogenesis and the menstrual cycle
nodes.essence: Sexual reproduction needs haploid gametes, made by meiosis, and a way to bring them together at the right time in a prepared place. The two sexes solve this differently.

nodes.title: Pregnancy, placenta and lactation
nodes.essence: Pregnancy is a 40-week experiment in which one organism builds another inside itself, half of it genetically foreign, and supplies all its oxygen, fuel and waste disposal across a single organ, the placenta, that the fetus grows for the purpose.

nodes.title: Fetal and neonatal physiology
nodes.essence: The fetus is not a small adult. It gets oxygen from a placenta, not lungs, so its circulation routes blood around the lungs and through the liver; its lungs are full of fluid; its temperature is the mother's; its glucose comes continuously by diffusion; its immunity is borrowed.
keyTerms: Ductus venosus, foramen ovale, ductus arteriosus
Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

nodes.title: Musculoskeletal system and skin
nodes.essence: This area is the body's interface with the physical world: the muscle that moves it, the skeleton and joints that give it shape and leverage and bear its loads, and the skin that separates it from the environment while sensing that environment and exchanging heat with it.

nodes.title: Skeletal muscle contraction and energetics
nodes.essence: Skeletal muscle is ~40% of body mass and the only tissue that converts chemical energy into movement on command. It does so with a molecular motor, myosin, that pulls on actin filaments in a repeating cycle powered by Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP) and switched on by calcium.

nodes.title: Bone remodelling and joints
nodes.essence: Bone looks inert and is the opposite: the adult skeleton is dissolved and rebuilt at ~10% of its mass a year, so that a bone is wholly replaced in about a decade.

nodes.title: The skin as barrier and sensor
nodes.essence: The skin is the largest organ, ~1.8 m² and ~15% of body weight, and it is the boundary condition for the rest of physiology.

nodes.title: Smooth muscle
nodes.essence: Smooth muscle lines every hollow organ and every blood vessel larger than a capillary, and it does a job skeletal muscle cannot: it holds tension for hours at a tiny energy cost, shortens to a fraction of its length, and answers to nerves, hormones, local metabolites and stretch at once.

nodes.title: Microbiology and Immunology
nodes.essence: This layer describes the boundary of the organism: the microbes that live on it, in it and against it, and the system that decides what to tolerate and what to destroy. It is placed as one layer because the immune system is defined by what it defends against.

nodes.title: Microbes and infection
nodes.essence: What lives on us, in us and against us, and how a few of those organisms cause disease.

nodes.title: Bacteria
nodes.essence: Bacteria are single-celled prokaryotes: a chromosome without a nucleus, a cytoplasm without organelles, a ribosome built differently from ours, and in most species a rigid cell wall that no human cell possesses. Two consequences of this design dominate medicine.

nodes.title: Viruses
nodes.essence: A virus is a genome in a protein coat, sometimes wrapped in a membrane stolen from its last host cell. It has no ribosomes, makes no energy and cannot replicate alone; it is a set of instructions that a living cell is tricked into executing.

nodes.title: Fungi, protozoa and helminths
nodes.essence: Fungi, protozoa and helminths are eukaryotes. Their cells are built like ours, so the chemical differences that make antibiotics selective mostly do not exist, and drugs against them are fewer and more toxic. Fungi are opportunists that mostly wait for immunity to fail.

nodes.title: The human microbiome
nodes.essence: A human body carries about as many bacterial cells as human ones, most of them in the colon, plus fungi, archaea and a vast population of bacteriophages. This community, the microbiome, is not a contaminant but an organ acquired at birth and shaped by diet, antibiotics and age.

nodes.title: Pathogenesis, virulence and toxins
nodes.essence: Pathogenesis is the sequence by which a microbe causes disease: it must reach a tissue, attach, obtain nutrients, avoid being killed, multiply, damage the host and leave to infect someone else.

nodes.title: Transmission and the chain of infection
nodes.essence: An infectious disease persists only if each case produces, on average, at least one more. The path from one host to the next is a chain with six links: an agent, a reservoir where it lives, a portal of exit, a mode of transmission, a portal of entry and a susceptible host.

nodes.title: Innate immunity
nodes.essence: How the body responds to a microbe in the first minutes and hours, before any cell specific for that microbe exists.

nodes.title: Barriers and pattern recognition
nodes.essence: The first defence is to keep microbes out; the second is to recognise, within minutes, that one has got in. Barriers stop the vast majority of encounters without any immune cell being involved, and most infections begin where a barrier has been breached.

nodes.title: Complement, phagocytes and the inflammatory cascade
nodes.essence: Once a microbe is recognised, the innate system must deliver killers to it. Two systems do this. Complement, ~30 plasma proteins activated by cascading proteolysis, coats the microbe for eating, punches holes in it and releases fragments that summon cells.

nodes.title: Cytokines, interferons and NK cells
nodes.essence: Immune cells coordinate by secreting small proteins, cytokines, that act on receptors of nearby cells and tell them what kind of threat has been found and what to do about it.

nodes.title: Adaptive immunity
nodes.essence: How vertebrates recognise any molecule they have never met, improve the response while it is happening, and remember it for life.

nodes.title: Antigen presentation and MHC
nodes.essence: T cells cannot see a microbe.

nodes.title: T cells
nodes.essence: T cells are the adaptive immune system's decision-makers and its assassins.

nodes.title: B cells and antibodies
nodes.essence: Antibodies are soluble receptors. A B cell makes one receptor by random gene rearrangement, and when antigen selects it the cell secretes that receptor into blood and secretions, where it binds the native surface of a microbe or toxin and marks it for destruction.

nodes.title: Immunological memory and vaccination
nodes.essence: Memory is what makes the adaptive system worth its slowness. A first encounter with a pathogen takes one to two weeks to produce useful antibody and T cells, which is long enough for most infections to cause disease.

nodes.title: Tolerance and self-recognition
nodes.essence: A system that makes receptors at random will make receptors against its own body; the price of being able to recognise anything is the risk of recognising yourself.

nodes.title: Immunity in disease
nodes.essence: What goes wrong with a system whose job is to tell self from non-self and harmless from dangerous, using receptors that are generated at random and patterns that are only approximately diagnostic.

nodes.title: Hypersensitivity and allergy
nodes.essence: Hypersensitivity is an adaptive immune response that damages the host out of proportion to the threat.

nodes.title: Autoimmunity
nodes.essence: Autoimmune disease is an adaptive immune response against the body's own antigens that causes damage.

nodes.title: Immunodeficiency
nodes.essence: Immunodeficiency is the absence or failure of a component of immunity, and it is the experiment that reveals what each component is for.

nodes.title: Transplant and tumour immunology
nodes.essence: Transplantation and cancer are the two problems in which medicine wants the immune system to make the opposite of its natural decision. A graft is non-self that must be tolerated; a tumour is self, slightly altered, that must be attacked.

nodes.title: Pathology
nodes.essence: Pathology is the study of disease as a biological process: what causes it, how the cause produces changes in cells and tissues, what those changes look like, and how they produce the symptoms a patient feels. This layer is general pathology.

nodes.title: Cell and tissue injury
nodes.essence: This area answers the first question of pathology: what happens to living tissue when something goes wrong, and how does the body respond?

nodes.title: Cell injury, adaptation and death
nodes.essence: Every disease begins as a cell that cannot keep up with what is asked of it. A stressed cell has three outcomes: it adapts (changes size, number or type), it is reversibly injured (swells and loses function but recovers if the stress stops) or it dies.

nodes.title: Acute inflammation
nodes.essence: Acute inflammation is the vascular and cellular response that delivers plasma proteins and leucocytes from the blood to a site of injury or infection within minutes to hours.

nodes.title: Chronic inflammation and granulomas
nodes.essence: Chronic inflammation is inflammation that lasts weeks to years because its cause is never removed: a microbe the body cannot kill, a foreign material it cannot digest, a self-antigen it cannot stop attacking, or a low-grade metabolic irritant it cannot switch off.

nodes.title: Tissue repair, regeneration and fibrosis
nodes.essence: After injury the body must refill the space that dead cells left. It has two ways: regeneration, replacing lost cells with the same kind from surviving cells or stem cells, and repair by connective tissue, filling the gap with a scar of collagen laid down by fibroblasts.

nodes.title: Haemodynamic disorders
nodes.essence: Cells live within a fraction of a millimetre of a capillary and depend on blood arriving, exchanging and leaving.

nodes.title: Oedema and fluid imbalance
nodes.essence: Oedema is excess fluid in the interstitial space or a body cavity. It forms whenever the forces that push fluid out of capillaries exceed the forces that pull it back, or the lymphatics that drain the surplus fail.

nodes.title: Thrombosis, embolism and infarction
nodes.essence: Haemostasis is a plug formed at the right place and time; thrombosis is the same plug formed in the wrong place, inside an intact vessel, where it obstructs flow.

nodes.title: Haemorrhage, shock and sepsis
nodes.essence: Shock is the failure of the circulation to deliver enough oxygen to the tissues, whatever the cause.

nodes.title: Atherosclerosis
nodes.essence: Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease of large and medium arteries in which cholesterol-carrying lipoprotein enters the wall, is modified, and provokes a macrophage-rich lesion (the atheroma or plaque) that grows for decades.

nodes.title: Neoplasia
nodes.essence: A neoplasm is a clone of the body's own cells that has escaped the controls governing its neighbours and grows autonomously.

nodes.title: Hallmarks of cancer
nodes.essence: A neoplasm is a clone of cells that grows without regard to the signals that govern its neighbours. Cancer is the malignant form: the clone also invades and spreads.

nodes.title: Oncogenes, tumour suppressors and genomic instability
nodes.essence: Cancer is a disease of the genome.

nodes.title: Invasion, metastasis and the tumour microenvironment
nodes.essence: Metastasis, the growth of a tumour at a site distant from its origin, causes about 90% of cancer deaths.

nodes.title: Causes of cancer
nodes.essence: Cancer is caused by mutations, and the causes of cancer are the things that make mutations or let mutated cells grow: chemicals, radiation, infectious agents, chronic inflammation, hormones, inherited susceptibility and, underlying all of them, the copying errors of normal cell division accumulating with age.

nodes.title: Tumour classification, grading and staging
nodes.essence: To treat a tumour one must answer three questions: what is it (classification), how abnormal does it look (grade), and how far has it spread (stage).

nodes.title: Genetic, metabolic and environmental disease
nodes.essence: The first three areas of this layer describe how tissue responds to injury, how the circulation fails and how a clone escapes control. This area asks where the injury comes from when it is built into the organism or delivered by the world around it.

nodes.title: Single-gene and chromosomal disorders
nodes.essence: Genetic disease spans a scale from one changed base to a whole extra chromosome.

nodes.title: Inborn errors of metabolism
nodes.essence: An inborn error of metabolism is an inherited deficiency of one enzyme or transporter in a metabolic pathway. Garrod coined the term in 1908 from alkaptonuria, the first disease traced to a single chemical step.

nodes.title: Nutritional disease, obesity and malnutrition
nodes.essence: Nutrition fails in two directions.

nodes.title: Environmental and toxic injury
nodes.essence: The environment injures through chemicals, physical agents and the substances people choose to consume. Roughly a quarter of global deaths are attributed to modifiable environmental factors, air pollution and tobacco foremost.

nodes.title: Diseases of aging and degeneration
nodes.essence: Aging is the progressive loss of the capacity to maintain and repair, and it is the largest risk factor for most of the diseases in this knowledge base: cardiovascular disease, cancer, dementia, osteoporosis, osteoarthritis and type 2 diabetes all rise steeply after 60.

nodes.title: Disease as process
nodes.essence: The four areas before this one describe mechanisms. This area describes the form a disease takes when those mechanisms are strung together in one patient over time, and how one thinks about a disease that has no single cause.

nodes.title: Aetiology, pathogenesis and natural history
nodes.essence: Every disease can be described in four linked terms: its aetiology (the cause), its pathogenesis (the sequence of events from cause to lesion), its morphology (the structural changes in cells and tissues) and its clinical manifestations (the symptoms, signs and test results those changes produce).

nodes.title: Multifactorial disease and risk
nodes.essence: Most common diseases have no single cause. Coronary disease, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, asthma, schizophrenia, most cancers and most birth defects arise from many genetic variants, each of small effect, interacting with many exposures over a lifetime.

nodes.title: Pharmacology and Therapeutics
nodes.essence: This layer is about intervention: what medicine can do to a body once it knows how the body works (layers 02–07) and how it fails (layer 08).

nodes.title: Pharmacokinetics
nodes.essence: Pharmacokinetics asks what the body does to a drug: how much of a dose reaches the blood, where it goes, how it is changed and how it leaves, and therefore what concentration the target will see at any moment after any regimen.

nodes.title: Absorption and bioavailability
nodes.essence: A drug acts only where it is, and most drugs are given somewhere other than their target. Absorption is the movement of a drug from its site of administration into the bloodstream; bioavailability (F) is the fraction of the given dose that arrives there unchanged.

nodes.title: Distribution and protein binding
nodes.essence: Once in plasma, a drug spreads into whatever tissues its chemistry allows and sits wherever it binds.

nodes.title: Drug metabolism and interactions
nodes.essence: The kidney excretes water-soluble molecules; most drugs are lipid-soluble, because that is what crosses membranes, so left alone they would be reabsorbed from the tubule and persist for weeks.

nodes.title: Elimination, half-life and dosing
nodes.essence: Most drugs leave the body at a rate proportional to how much is present, so their concentration decays exponentially with a characteristic half-life.

nodes.title: Pharmacokinetics across the life course
nodes.essence: The equations of pharmacokinetics do not change with age, but every parameter in them does.

nodes.title: Pharmacodynamics
nodes.essence: Pharmacodynamics asks what a drug does to the body once it is there: how a concentration at a target becomes an effect, how the size of that effect depends on concentration, how it changes with time and repeated exposure, how it differs between people, and when it becomes harm.

nodes.title: Receptor theory, agonists and antagonists
nodes.essence: Most drugs work by binding to a protein the body already uses for its own signalling, and what happens next depends on two separable properties: how tightly the drug binds (affinity) and what it does to the protein once bound (efficacy).
keyTerms: Agonist, partial agonist, antagonist, inverse agonist

nodes.title: Dose–response and therapeutic index
nodes.essence: There are two different dose–response curves and confusing them causes errors. The graded curve describes one system: as concentration rises, the magnitude of effect rises along the sigmoid that receptor theory predicts, until it saturates.

nodes.title: Tolerance, dependence and withdrawal
nodes.essence: A living system that is pushed in one direction pushes back. Give a drug continuously and the tissue adapts to its presence: receptors are removed or uncoupled, opposing pathways are upregulated, metabolism accelerates, so that the same dose produces less effect (tolerance).

nodes.title: Adverse drug reactions and pharmacovigilance
nodes.essence: Every drug that does something can do something unwanted. Most adverse drug reactions (ADRs) are the drug's known pharmacology appearing in the wrong tissue, at the wrong dose or in the wrong patient; these are predictable, dose-related and common.

nodes.title: Pharmacogenomics and individual variation
nodes.essence: The quantal dose–response curve is wide because people differ, and much of that difference is inherited.

nodes.title: Drug classes by mechanism
nodes.essence: There are several thousand licensed drugs and a few dozen mechanisms.

nodes.title: Autonomic and cardiovascular drugs
nodes.essence: The circulation is controlled by a handful of signals (noradrenaline and adrenaline on adrenoceptors, acetylcholine on muscarinic receptors, angiotensin II and aldosterone, nitric oxide) acting on a handful of effectors (heart rate, contractility, vascular tone, blood volume).

nodes.title: Central nervous system drugs
nodes.essence: Drugs that act on the brain and spinal cord do so at synapses and ion channels, the same sites that physiology uses to compute.

nodes.title: Antimicrobials
nodes.essence: An antimicrobial is a poison with a difference: it must kill or arrest a microbe inside a human while leaving the human alone.

nodes.title: Anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory drugs
nodes.essence: Inflammation is one response with many triggers, and its chemistry runs through a few hubs: arachidonic acid metabolites (prostaglandins, leukotrienes), the cytokines that coordinate leukocytes (tumour necrosis factor (TNF), the interleukins), the glucocorticoid-sensitive transcription programme that drives most of it, and the T-cell activation and lymphocyte proliferation that sustain adaptive attack.

nodes.title: Anticancer drugs
nodes.essence: A cancer cell is a human cell, so there is no wall or ribosome to attack; the differences are quantitative (it divides more, repairs DNA worse, depends on particular signals) or specific to the mutations that made it.

nodes.title: Endocrine and metabolic drugs
nodes.essence: Endocrine drugs are the simplest class to reason about and the easiest to get wrong, because every hormone sits in a feedback loop.

nodes.title: Biologics and advanced therapies
nodes.essence: Small-molecule drugs are limited to targets with a pocket they can fit, roughly enzymes, channels and receptors with ligand sites, which is perhaps a tenth of the proteome.

nodes.title: Non-drug therapeutics
nodes.essence: Most of what medicine does to patients is not a drug. It cuts, irradiates, implants, infuses and persuades, and each of these has a mechanism as definite as a receptor's.

nodes.title: Principles of surgery and wound care
nodes.essence: Surgery is controlled injury. The surgeon cuts to remove what is diseased, reconnect what is separated, relieve what is obstructed or replace what is lost, and then depends on the body to heal the wound that this leaves.
keyTerms: Primary, secondary and delayed primary intention

nodes.title: Radiotherapy and radiation biology
nodes.essence: Ionising radiation kills cells by breaking DNA, and radiotherapy is the art of breaking enough DNA in a tumour while sparing the normal tissue around it.

nodes.title: Devices, implants and biomaterials
nodes.essence: A device does mechanically, electrically or structurally what a drug cannot: it bears load, holds a lumen open, replaces a valve, paces a heart, filters blood or converts sound into nerve impulses.

nodes.title: Fluids, nutrition and blood products
nodes.essence: Water, salt, fuel and blood are the oldest therapies and the ones most often given carelessly, because they feel like replacement rather than treatment.

nodes.title: Behaviour change and the placebo effect
nodes.essence: Most of the burden of disease in rich countries is driven by what people do (smoke, eat, drink, move, sleep, take or not take their medicines), and most treatments depend on a patient doing something for months.

nodes.title: Drug development and toxicology
nodes.essence: The rest of the layer describes drugs that exist and work at doses that help. This area describes the two boundaries of that territory: how a molecule earns the right to be called a drug, and what happens when any substance, drug or not, is taken past the point where it helps.

nodes.title: From target to approval
nodes.essence: A drug is a hypothesis: that changing the activity of one protein will change the course of a disease in people, safely, at a dose they can take.

nodes.title: Toxicology and poisoning
nodes.essence: Paracelsus's rule, that the dose makes the poison, is the whole of toxicology in one sentence: every substance has a dose–response curve for harm, and a poison is any substance taken to the point on that curve where harm begins.

nodes.title: Epidemiology and Evidence
nodes.essence: Everything below this layer describes a body: how it is built, how it works, how it fails, and what a drug does to it.

nodes.title: Epidemiology
nodes.essence: Epidemiology is the study of how disease is distributed in populations and of what determines that distribution. It answers questions no examination of a single patient can: how common is this condition, who gets it, what raises or lowers the risk, and is a rise in cases real?

nodes.title: Measures of frequency and association
nodes.essence: Epidemiology counts. Before anyone can ask whether smoking causes lung cancer or whether a drug prevents stroke, someone must say how often the disease occurs, in whom, and how that frequency differs between people with and without an exposure.

nodes.title: Observational study designs
nodes.essence: Most questions in medicine cannot be answered by experiment. Nobody can randomise people to smoke, to be poor or to carry a gene, and rare harms of a drug appear only after a million people have taken it.

nodes.title: Bias, confounding and chance
nodes.essence: An observed association between an exposure and a disease has four possible explanations: the exposure causes the disease; the study selected or measured its subjects in a way that manufactured the association (bias); a third factor causes both (confounding); or random variation produced it (chance).

nodes.title: Infectious disease dynamics
nodes.essence: Infectious disease breaks the assumption behind the rest of epidemiology: that one person's risk is independent of another's. Whether you catch influenza depends on how many people around you have it, so the incidence of an infection depends on its own prevalence.

nodes.title: Surveillance and outbreak investigation
nodes.essence: Surveillance is epidemiology run continuously: the systematic collection, analysis and interpretation of health data, linked to the people who can act on them.

nodes.title: Evidence-based medicine
nodes.essence: Epidemiology asks what causes disease; evidence-based medicine asks what to do about it, and how sure we can be.

nodes.title: Randomized controlled trials
nodes.essence: The Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT) is the one study design that answers "does this treatment work?" without having to know what else differs between treated and untreated people. Its trick is to let a coin, not a doctor or a patient, decide who gets the treatment.

nodes.title: Diagnostic accuracy studies
nodes.essence: A diagnostic test is a measurement whose result is used to change the probability that a patient has a condition.

nodes.title: Systematic reviews and meta-analysis
nodes.essence: No single trial settles a question. Trials are small, their populations differ, and chance scatters their results around the truth.

nodes.title: Grading evidence and guidelines
nodes.essence: Evidence-based medicine, as Sackett defined it in 1996, is the integration of the best available research evidence with clinical expertise and the patient's values.
keyTerms: Risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias

nodes.title: Research integrity and publication bias
nodes.essence: The published literature is not a random sample of the research that was done. Studies with positive, striking results are more likely to be completed, submitted, accepted, published quickly and cited; studies that find nothing are more likely to vanish.
keyTerms: p-hacking and the garden of forking paths

nodes.title: Screening and prevention
nodes.essence: Everything else in this layer measures disease after it has happened. This area asks how to intervene before it does: by removing causes, by finding disease in its silent phase, or by identifying the people most likely to develop it.

nodes.title: Levels of prevention
nodes.essence: Every disease has a natural history: a period of exposure and susceptibility, a preclinical phase in which the process is under way but silent, a clinical phase, and an outcome.

nodes.title: Screening principles and biases
nodes.essence: Screening is the application of a test to people without symptoms in order to find disease earlier than it would have presented, on the assumption that earlier treatment changes the outcome.

nodes.title: Risk prediction and stratification
nodes.essence: A risk prediction model takes what is known about a person now (age, sex, blood pressure, smoking, a biomarker, a genotype) and returns the probability of an outcome over a stated horizon: a 10-year risk of cardiovascular disease, a 30-day risk of death after surgery, the probability that a chest pain is a myocardial infarction.

nodes.title: Clinical Method and Diagnostics
nodes.essence: Every layer so far has been about disease in general or in populations. This layer is about one patient, now.

nodes.title: The clinical encounter
nodes.essence: A patient arrives with a complaint. Within an hour, often within minutes, a clinician must decide what is probably wrong, how dangerous it is, whether a test would help, what to do, and what to tell the patient about what lies ahead. This area is the method by which that is done.

nodes.title: History taking and communication
nodes.essence: The history is the patient's account of what has happened to them, obtained and structured by the clinician.
keyTerms: Past medical, drug, family and social history

nodes.title: Physical examination and signs
nodes.essence: A physical sign is a change in the body that an examiner can detect with the senses, sometimes aided by a simple instrument.

nodes.title: Clinical reasoning and cognitive bias
nodes.essence: Clinical reasoning is the process by which a clinician moves from a patient's presentation to a working diagnosis and a decision, under uncertainty and usually under time pressure.

nodes.title: Using tests, pre-test probability and thresholds
nodes.essence: A test is worth ordering only if its result could change what you do. That single sentence contains the whole theory of testing. Before the test there is a probability of disease, set by prevalence and the history and examination.

nodes.title: Prognosis and shared decision-making
nodes.essence: Diagnosis says what is wrong; prognosis says what will happen, with and without each possible action. It is a probability statement about the future, derived from cohorts of similar patients and adjusted to the person in front of you.
keyTerms: Absolute risk reduction and Number Needed to Treat (NNT)

nodes.title: Laboratory medicine
nodes.essence: The encounter yields what the clinician can see, hear and feel. Laboratory medicine yields what they cannot: the concentration of potassium, the number and shape of red cells, the organism in the blood, the architecture of a biopsy.

nodes.title: Clinical chemistry and reference ranges
nodes.essence: Clinical chemistry measures the concentrations of substances in blood, urine and other fluids, and most of medicine's routine numbers (sodium, potassium, creatinine, glucose, bilirubin, troponin) come from it.

nodes.title: Haematology and coagulation testing
nodes.essence: Blood is the one tissue that can be sampled from every patient in a minute, and the full blood count is the most frequently performed test in medicine.

nodes.title: Microbiological and serological diagnosis
nodes.essence: To treat an infection well you need to know which organism is present, whether it is the cause or a bystander, and what will kill it.

nodes.title: Histopathology, cytology and molecular diagnostics
nodes.essence: Histopathology is the examination of tissue under the microscope, and for most cancers and many inflammatory diseases it is the diagnosis: the final word on whether a lesion is malignant, what kind, how aggressive, and whether it has been removed.

nodes.title: Imaging and physiological measurement
nodes.essence: The examination reaches as far as the senses; the laboratory needs a sample.

nodes.title: Radiography and computed tomography
nodes.essence: An X-ray image is a shadow. A beam of high-energy photons passes through the body, tissues absorb or scatter them in proportion to their density and atomic number, and a detector on the far side records what got through.

nodes.title: Ultrasound
nodes.essence: Ultrasound is echolocation. A transducer sends a short pulse of sound at megahertz frequencies into the body, listens for echoes, and places each echo at a depth given by half the round-trip time multiplied by the speed of sound in tissue (about 1,540 m/s).

nodes.title: Magnetic resonance imaging
nodes.essence: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) makes pictures from the hydrogen nuclei in the body's water and fat.

nodes.title: Nuclear medicine and molecular imaging
nodes.essence: Every other imaging method sends energy into the body and reads what comes back.
keyTerms: Hybrid imaging (PET-CT, Single-Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT)-CT)

nodes.title: Electrocardiography and electrophysiological testing
nodes.essence: Excitable cells generate currents when they depolarise, and the body is a conductor, so those currents produce voltages at the skin.
keyTerms: P wave, QRS complex, T wave

nodes.title: Functional testing: spirometry, exercise and sleep
nodes.essence: Imaging shows what an organ looks like; functional testing measures what it can do.
keyTerms: Forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1)
Peak oxygen uptake (VO2 max, where VO2 is the rate of oxygen consumption)

nodes.title: Organ-System Specialties
nodes.essence: This layer is the first in which the tree talks about diseases as a clinician meets them: a patient with breathlessness, a raised creatinine, a seizure, a rash.

nodes.title: Cardiology
nodes.essence: Cardiology is the medicine of a pump and its pipes.

nodes.title: Ischaemic heart disease
nodes.essence: Ischaemic heart disease is a supply–demand failure in a muscle that cannot pause. The myocardium extracts about 70% of the oxygen in coronary blood at rest, so it has almost no extraction reserve and must meet any rise in demand by increasing flow.

nodes.title: Heart failure
nodes.essence: Heart failure is not a disease but a syndrome: the heart cannot deliver the output the body needs at normal filling pressures, and the body's response to that shortfall becomes the main driver of the illness.

nodes.title: Arrhythmias
nodes.essence: An arrhythmia is a failure of the heart's timing system: too slow, too fast, or disorganised.

nodes.title: Valvular and structural heart disease
nodes.essence: Valvular and structural heart disease is cardiology as plumbing.

nodes.title: Hypertension and vascular disease
nodes.essence: Hypertension is a regulated variable set too high. Arterial pressure is cardiac output times peripheral resistance, and the kidney, the sympathetic nervous system and the renin–angiotensin system hold it at a set point over hours to years.

nodes.title: Pulmonology
nodes.essence: Pulmonology is the medicine of gas exchange, and the lung can fail at exactly four places: air cannot get in and out (airways), the gas-exchanging tissue is thickened or destroyed (interstitium and alveoli), the alveoli are filled with something other than air (infection, fluid, blood), or blood does not reach ventilated alveoli (the pulmonary circulation).

nodes.title: Asthma and COPD
nodes.essence: Asthma and Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) are the two diseases of expiratory airflow limitation: the same obstructive pattern on spirometry, differing in what narrows the airway and whether it opens again.

nodes.title: Interstitial and restrictive lung disease
nodes.essence: Restrictive lung disease is the mirror of obstruction: the lung can empty but cannot fill.

nodes.title: Pneumonia and respiratory infections
nodes.essence: The lung inhales about 10,000 litres of unsterile air a day across a surface the size of a tennis court, so respiratory infection is the commonest infection and pneumonia the commonest infectious cause of death.

nodes.title: Pulmonary vascular disease and respiratory failure
nodes.essence: This leaf covers the lung's blood supply and the end state of every lung disease.

nodes.title: Nephrology
nodes.essence: Nephrology is the medicine of the organ that keeps the internal environment constant.

nodes.title: Acute kidney injury
nodes.essence: Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) is a fall in glomerular filtration over hours to days, detected as a rising creatinine or a falling urine output.

nodes.title: Chronic kidney disease and dialysis
nodes.essence: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is the loss of nephrons over months to years, with no capacity to make new ones.

nodes.title: Glomerular and tubular diseases
nodes.essence: These are the diseases of the nephron itself rather than of its blood supply or outflow.

nodes.title: Electrolyte and acid–base disorders
nodes.essence: Electrolyte and acid–base disorders are failures of regulation, and the regulated variables are few: the sodium concentration (which is really the body's water), the potassium concentration (which is really the ratio of potassium inside cells to outside), the calcium concentration, and the hydrogen ion concentration.

nodes.title: Gastroenterology and hepatology
nodes.essence: Gastroenterology and hepatology cover a nine-metre tube and the three glands that drain into it.

nodes.title: Acid-peptic disease and GI bleeding
nodes.essence: The stomach secretes hydrochloric acid to a pH of 1–2 and the protease pepsin, and does not digest itself only because a mucus–bicarbonate layer, tight epithelial junctions, rapid cell turnover and a rich blood flow defend the mucosa.

nodes.title: Inflammatory bowel disease and malabsorption
nodes.essence: The intestinal wall must do two opposite things across one cell layer: absorb nutrients and exclude a microbial population of some 10^13 cells.

nodes.title: Liver disease
nodes.essence: The liver is the organ with the greatest reserve and the greatest capacity to regenerate, and liver disease is the story of both being exhausted.

nodes.title: Pancreatic and biliary disease
nodes.essence: The pancreas and the biliary tree share a duct, an opening into the duodenum, and a set of diseases that follow from that anatomy.

nodes.title: Endocrinology
nodes.essence: Endocrinology is the medicine of chemical control.

nodes.title: Diabetes mellitus
nodes.essence: Diabetes mellitus is chronic hyperglycaemia from a failure of insulin: absent (type 1, autoimmune destruction of the beta cells), or insufficient for a body that has become resistant to it (type 2, which is over 90% of cases).

nodes.title: Thyroid disease
nodes.essence: Thyroid hormone sets the metabolic rate of nearly every cell, and the thyroid is the gland that shows the logic of endocrinology most clearly: a single hormone, a single controller (Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH) from the pituitary), a tight negative feedback loop, and diseases that are too little, too much, a lump, or a cancer.

nodes.title: Adrenal, pituitary and gonadal disorders
nodes.essence: The pituitary is a pea-sized gland that controls the thyroid, the adrenal cortex, the gonads, growth and lactation, and sits in a bony pocket beneath the optic chiasm.

nodes.title: Obesity, lipids and metabolic syndrome
nodes.essence: Obesity is the storage of more energy as fat than the body can hold without harm, and it is now the upstream cause of much of the disease in this layer.

nodes.title: Bone and calcium disorders
nodes.essence: The skeleton is two things at once: a structure that must bear load, and the body's store of calcium and phosphate, from which the plasma calcium is defended minute by minute. The two roles conflict.

nodes.title: Haematology
nodes.essence: Haematology is the medicine of a liquid organ. Blood is made continuously in the marrow, destroyed and replaced at a rate that keeps its composition constant, and carries a clotting system poised to seal a wound and inhibitors poised to stop it.

nodes.title: Anaemias
nodes.essence: Anaemia is a haemoglobin concentration too low to carry the oxygen the tissues demand, and it is a sign, not a diagnosis.

nodes.title: Bleeding and clotting disorders
nodes.essence: Haemostasis must do two opposite things: seal a hole within minutes and never clot inside an intact vessel.

nodes.title: Haematological malignancies
nodes.essence: Haematological malignancies are cancers of blood-forming and immune cells, and their behaviour follows from the biology of the cell that went wrong. Haematopoiesis is a hierarchy from stem cell to mature cell, and a mutation can arrest a clone at any rung.

nodes.title: Transfusion medicine
nodes.essence: Transfusion is a transplant of liquid tissue, and everything about it follows from that.

nodes.title: Oncology
nodes.essence: Oncology is the one organ-system specialty defined by a disease process rather than an organ.

nodes.title: Principles of cancer care
nodes.essence: Cancer care answers one question in sequence: what is this tumour, where has it reached, what does the patient want, and which combination of cutting, burning and poisoning best serves that goal at acceptable cost?

nodes.title: Systemic anticancer therapy
nodes.essence: Systemic therapy is the only treatment that reaches cancer cells wherever they are, and its history is a search for ever-smaller differences between tumour and host to exploit.

nodes.title: Common solid tumours
nodes.essence: Five sites, lung, breast, colorectum, prostate and skin, account for roughly half of all cancers in high-income countries (2020s), and together they illustrate every principle of oncology.

nodes.title: Infectious diseases
