nodes.essence: Infectious diseases is the specialty of the host's encounter with another organism. Like oncology, it is defined by a process rather than an organ, so it reaches into every other specialty: a pneumonia is pulmonology, a meningitis is neurology, and both are infectious diseases.

nodes.title: Fever and sepsis
nodes.essence: Fever is a regulated rise in the temperature set point, triggered by cytokines, and is a sign of inflammation, not specifically of infection.

nodes.title: Antimicrobial stewardship
nodes.essence: Antimicrobials are the only drugs whose use by one patient reduces their value for everyone else, because every course selects for resistant organisms that spread.

nodes.title: HIV and chronic viral infections
nodes.essence: Some viruses are never cleared.

nodes.title: Tuberculosis and tropical infections
nodes.essence: Tuberculosis, malaria and the helminths are the infections of poverty, and together they kill or disable more people than any other group of pathogens outside pandemics.

nodes.title: Infection control and healthcare-associated infection
nodes.essence: A hospital concentrates the sickest, most immunosuppressed people in one building, pierces their barriers with cannulas, catheters and tubes, clears their protective flora with antibiotics, and moves staff between them hundreds of times a day.
keyTerms: Standard, contact, droplet and airborne precautions

nodes.title: Rheumatology and clinical immunology
nodes.essence: Rheumatology began as the medicine of painful joints and became the medicine of the immune system attacking the self, because the commonest cause of destructive joint disease turned out to be autoimmune.

nodes.title: Inflammatory arthritis
nodes.essence: Inflammatory arthritis is the synovium turned into a chronically inflamed, invasive tissue that destroys the joint it was meant to lubricate.

nodes.title: Connective tissue disease and vasculitis
nodes.essence: The connective tissue diseases and the vasculitides are systemic autoimmunity aimed at targets present in every organ: nuclear components, the endothelium, the vessel wall, the fibroblast.

nodes.title: Osteoarthritis, gout and regional pain
nodes.essence: Most musculoskeletal pain is not autoimmune. Osteoarthritis is the failure of a joint as a mechanical organ: cartilage worn faster than it is repaired, bone remodelling in response, and pain from the innervated tissues around a cartilage that has none.

nodes.title: Allergy and immunodeficiency in practice
nodes.essence: Clinical immunology sees the immune system fail in two opposite directions: too much response to the harmless (allergy) and too little to the dangerous (immunodeficiency).

nodes.title: Neurology
nodes.essence: Neurology is the medicine of the organ that cannot be biopsied, barely regenerates and does something different in every cubic centimetre. Because function is localised, a lesion's position can be inferred from what has been lost: the examination answers "where" before "what".

nodes.title: Stroke
nodes.essence: A stroke is a sudden focal loss of brain function caused by a blocked or burst blood vessel. The brain uses a fifth of the body's oxygen with almost no stored fuel, so neurons downstream of an occluded artery stop firing within seconds and die within minutes (supply and demand).

nodes.title: Epilepsy
nodes.essence: A seizure is a transient episode of abnormal, excessive, synchronised neuronal firing; epilepsy is the enduring tendency to have them.

nodes.title: Headache
nodes.essence: Headache is the commonest neurological complaint and the brain itself is never its source: the brain has no pain receptors, so head pain comes from meninges, vessels, muscles, sinuses, eyes and teeth, almost all routed through the trigeminal nerve.

nodes.title: Neurodegenerative disease
nodes.essence: The neurodegenerative diseases are the slow death of selected neurons, and nearly all are diseases of protein folding.

nodes.title: Demyelinating and neuromuscular disease
nodes.essence: Movement requires a chain: motor neuron, the myelin that insulates it, the neuromuscular junction and muscle; sensation runs the same chain in reverse.

nodes.title: Dermatology
nodes.essence: Dermatology is the medicine of the largest organ and the only one examined completely without instruments.

nodes.title: Skin lesion morphology and diagnosis
nodes.essence: The skin is the only organ examined directly, in its entirety, with the naked eye, and dermatology is built on a disciplined way of describing what is seen.

nodes.title: Inflammatory skin disease
nodes.essence: The inflammatory skin diseases are the skin's two jobs, barrier and immune sentinel, going wrong together.

nodes.title: Skin cancer and skin infections
nodes.essence: The skin faces the two external hazards no other organ meets directly: ultraviolet radiation and the microbial world.

nodes.title: Acute, Perioperative and Procedural Care
nodes.essence: The organ-system specialties of layer 12 are organised by which system fails. This layer is organised by how fast it fails and by what is done with the hands. Its five branches share one subject: physiology under stress, measured against time.

nodes.title: Surgery
nodes.essence: Surgery treats disease by changing anatomy: removing what is diseased, repairing what is broken, draining what is contained, bypassing what is blocked, replacing what is lost. The price is that every operation is itself an injury.

nodes.title: The surgical decision
nodes.essence: An operation is a deliberate injury accepted because the disease it removes, repairs or bypasses is worse. The body cannot tell a scalpel from a knife: both provoke the same acute inflammation, the same neuroendocrine stress response and the same programme of repair.

nodes.title: The acute abdomen
nodes.essence: The acute abdomen is sudden abdominal pain severe enough to raise the question of an operation. The abdomen is a closed cavity lined by peritoneum and filled with hollow tubes under pressure, solid organs under perfusion and a litre of bacteria behind a single epithelial layer.

nodes.title: Trauma and haemorrhage control
nodes.essence: Trauma is injury by energy. Kinetic energy (½mv²) delivered to tissue tears, crushes and shears it; the body's reply is bleeding, then shock, then a coagulopathy that makes the bleeding worse.

nodes.title: Orthopaedics, fractures and joints
nodes.essence: Orthopaedics is surgery of the load-bearing frame: bone, cartilage, ligament, tendon and the joints they form.

nodes.title: Surgical subspecialties
nodes.essence: General surgery split into subspecialties during the twentieth century for two reasons: anatomy, because the techniques for a coronary artery, a brain and a kidney have little in common, and volume, because outcomes for complex operations improve with the number a team performs.

nodes.title: Urology
nodes.essence: Urology is the surgery of a plumbing system: two filters, two tubes, a muscular reservoir and an outflow that in men passes through a gland that grows for life. Nearly everything the specialty treats is one of four events in that system.

nodes.title: Burns
nodes.essence: A burn is a wound that becomes a systemic disease when it is large enough. Heat, chemicals or electricity kill skin in proportion to temperature and time, and dead skin is a barrier lost to water, heat and bacteria.

nodes.title: Anaesthesia and perioperative medicine
nodes.essence: Before 1846 an operation was limited by how long a conscious patient could bear it.

nodes.title: General and regional anaesthesia
nodes.essence: Anaesthesia is the reversible removal of four things an operation would otherwise provoke: consciousness, the perception of pain, movement, and the autonomic reflexes that make the heart race and the pressure climb under the knife.

nodes.title: Airway and ventilation management
nodes.essence: The airway is the first thing an anaesthetic takes away and the first thing that kills when it is lost.

nodes.title: Perioperative risk and complications
nodes.essence: Most people who die after an operation die of a medical illness that the operation provoked: a myocardial infarction, a pneumonia, a pulmonary embolus, a kidney that stopped, a delirium that led to a fall.

nodes.title: Critical care
nodes.essence: Critical care, delivered in the Intensive Care Unit (ICU), is the branch of medicine that keeps a patient alive while the cause of their collapse is found and treated.

nodes.title: Shock and haemodynamic support
nodes.essence: Shock is not low blood pressure. It is the state in which oxygen delivery to tissues falls below their consumption, so cells switch to anaerobic metabolism, lactate accumulates and organs begin to fail (pathology of shock).

nodes.title: Respiratory failure and mechanical ventilation
nodes.essence: The lung does two separable jobs: it loads oxygen onto blood and it unloads carbon dioxide. Respiratory failure is the failure of either, and the two fail for different reasons, show different gases and need different support.

nodes.title: Sepsis and multi-organ failure
nodes.essence: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection (the 2016 consensus definition). The emphasis is deliberate: the microbe starts it, but the damage is done by the body's own inflammatory cascade running without its usual limits.

nodes.title: Organ support and ICU syndromes
nodes.essence: Once the circulation and the lungs are supported, the rest of the body still has to be kept alive for days or weeks: the kidney that stopped, the gut that will not absorb, the brain that must tolerate a tube, the muscles that waste while the patient lies still.

nodes.title: Emergency medicine
nodes.essence: Emergency medicine is defined not by an organ or a disease but by a time window and a state of ignorance. The patient arrives undifferentiated: a collapse, a pain, a breathlessness, with no diagnosis, often no history, and a clock that may be running in seconds.

nodes.title: Triage and the ABCDE approach
nodes.essence: When many patients arrive with unknown problems, two sorting decisions must be made before any diagnosis: which patient first, and within that patient, which problem first. Triage answers the first by estimating time to harm from a few physiological variables.

nodes.title: Resuscitation and cardiac arrest
nodes.essence: Cardiac arrest is the cessation of effective cardiac output: no pulse, no perfusion, unconsciousness within seconds and, without intervention, irreversible brain injury within minutes.

nodes.title: Poisoning and overdose
nodes.essence: Poisoning is pharmacology past the top of the dose–response curve.

nodes.title: Prehospital and disaster medicine
nodes.essence: Most time-critical physiology fails outside a hospital, and the interval before the hospital is where survival from cardiac arrest, haemorrhage and stroke is largely decided.
keyTerms: Scoop and run versus stay and play

nodes.title: Ophthalmology and ENT
nodes.essence: The sense organs are small, anatomically dense and functionally precious: a few cubic centimetres of tissue carry sight, hearing, balance, smell, voice, swallowing and the upper airway.

nodes.title: The eye and vision loss
nodes.essence: The eye is a camera attached to a piece of brain. Light is refracted by the cornea and lens onto the retina, where photoreceptors transduce it and three layers of neurons compress it into the optic nerve.

nodes.title: The ear, hearing and balance
nodes.essence: The ear solves two physics problems.

nodes.title: Nose, throat and head and neck
nodes.essence: The nose, pharynx and larynx are the shared entrance to the lungs and the gut: air and food cross in the pharynx, and the larynx exists to keep them apart while also producing the voice.

nodes.title: Life course, mind and integrative care
nodes.essence: The specialties of layer 12 each own an organ system and those of layer 13 own an acute setting or a technique.

nodes.title: Paediatrics
nodes.essence: Paediatrics is medicine for a body that is still being built. Every organ system of layer 12 and every acute problem of layer 13 occurs in children, but in a host whose physiology, anatomy, pharmacology, immunity and capacity to consent change month by month.

nodes.title: The newborn and neonatology
nodes.essence: Birth is the most abrupt physiological transition a human ever makes: in a few minutes an organism that obtained oxygen, glucose and warmth from the placenta must breathe, perfuse its own lungs, burn its own fuel and hold its own temperature.

nodes.title: Growth, development and the child as patient
nodes.essence: A child is an organism under construction, so the central paediatric question is not only "is this child ill?" but "is this child growing and developing along its expected path?" Growth (gain in size) and development (gain in function) follow predictable trajectories whose deviation is the earliest sign of chronic disease, neglect or genetic disorder, often long before any symptom.

nodes.title: Common childhood illness
nodes.essence: Most childhood illness is infection meeting a host that has not yet met the organism: a child acquires six to ten respiratory infections a year while its adaptive immune memory is being written.

nodes.title: Congenital and genetic disease in childhood
nodes.essence: About 2–3% of babies are born with a major structural malformation, and a comparable fraction carry a single-gene or chromosomal disorder that will declare itself in childhood.

nodes.title: Adolescent health and safeguarding
nodes.essence: Adolescence is the second great developmental transition, from the dependent child to the autonomous adult, driven by puberty in the body and by a brain whose reward and emotional systems mature years before its executive control.

nodes.title: Obstetrics and gynaecology
nodes.essence: Obstetrics and gynaecology is the medicine of the female reproductive system across the life course, and of the one physiological state, pregnancy, in which a clinician has two patients inside one body.

nodes.title: Pregnancy and its complications
nodes.essence: Pregnancy is a nine-month physiological experiment in which one organism grows another inside itself, and most of its complications are the experiment's control systems pushed past their limits.

nodes.title: Labour, delivery and the puerperium
nodes.essence: Labour is a positive-feedback process that expels a fetus through a bony pelvis that evolution made barely wide enough, followed by the most dangerous hour of a woman's reproductive life, when a placental bed the size of a dinner plate must stop bleeding by muscular contraction alone.

nodes.title: Gynaecological disease
nodes.essence: The female reproductive tract is an organ system that rebuilds itself every month under hormonal command, which makes its diseases unusually legible: most are either tissue responding to oestrogen in the wrong place or amount (fibroids, endometriosis, endometrial cancer), a hormonal axis that has stopped cycling (polycystic ovary syndrome, amenorrhoea), an infection ascending from the vagina (pelvic inflammatory disease, and the papillomavirus behind cervical cancer), or a structural failure of the pelvic floor after childbirth.

nodes.title: Fertility, contraception and menopause
nodes.essence: Reproduction is controlled by one hormonal axis, hypothalamus to pituitary to gonad, and this leaf is about managing that axis in three directions: switching conception on when it fails (fertility medicine), switching it off reliably when it is unwanted (contraception), and managing its permanent shutdown (menopause).

nodes.title: Psychiatry
nodes.essence: Psychiatry is the medicine of disorders of mood, thought, perception, behaviour and the control of appetite and impulse: the properties of a whole person rather than of an organ.

nodes.title: The mental state and psychiatric formulation
nodes.essence: Psychiatry has no biopsy, no blood test and no scan that makes a diagnosis; its examination is the mental state, a structured observation of how a person appears, speaks, feels, thinks, perceives and understands, taken alongside a history that reaches back into childhood and outward into relationships and circumstances.

nodes.title: Mood and anxiety disorders
nodes.essence: Depression and anxiety are the commonest mental disorders and, by years lived with disability, among the largest causes of ill health in the world.

nodes.title: Psychosis
nodes.essence: Psychosis is a loss of contact with shared reality: beliefs held with certainty against all evidence (delusions), perceptions without stimulus (hallucinations, most often voices) and disorganised thought.

nodes.title: Addiction and substance use
nodes.essence: Addiction is compulsive use of a substance or pursuit of a behaviour despite harm, with loss of control over it.

nodes.title: Neurodevelopmental, personality and eating disorders
nodes.essence: Three groups of disorders are defined less by episodes than by the shape of a person: neurodevelopmental conditions (autism, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, intellectual disability) in which the brain develops along an atypical path from early life; personality disorders in which enduring patterns of feeling, relating and behaving cause persistent distress or harm; and eating disorders in which the control of eating and weight becomes the organising principle of a life and starvation does the physical damage.

nodes.title: Geriatrics and palliative care
nodes.essence: This area is the medicine of the end of the life course: the older person whose reserve has run low, the person of any age whose illness will not be cured, and the process of dying itself.

nodes.title: Frailty, multimorbidity and polypharmacy
nodes.essence: Ageing narrows the margin between the body's capacity and the demands placed on it, in every organ at once.

nodes.title: Geriatric syndromes
nodes.essence: A geriatric syndrome is a clinical presentation in an older person that has many contributing causes across several systems and does not fit a single organ's disease: delirium, falls, incontinence, immobility, pressure injury and the cognitive decline of dementia.
keyTerms: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia

nodes.title: Palliative care and symptom control
nodes.essence: Palliative care is medicine whose target is the person's experience rather than the disease's course: the relief of pain, breathlessness, nausea, delirium and distress in people with life-limiting illness, from diagnosis to death.

nodes.title: Death, dying and end-of-life decisions
nodes.essence: Every patient dies, and in high-income countries most now die slowly, of chronic disease, in old age, in a hospital or care home, after a series of decisions about which treatments to start, continue and stop.

nodes.title: Primary care and integration
nodes.essence: This area is about the parts of medicine defined by the whole person rather than by any disease: the generalist who is the first contact and the constant across a lifetime, the long management of chronic disease that happens mostly in the patient's own hands, the restoration of function after the lesion is fixed, the exposures of exercise, work and daily living, and, finally, the structure of the specialty graph itself.

nodes.title: Family medicine and the generalist
nodes.essence: Family medicine (general practice) is the specialty defined not by an organ, a process, an age or a setting but by a relationship: one clinician, or one team, responsible for a person's whole health over time, for whatever they bring, as the first point of contact.

nodes.title: Chronic disease and self-management
nodes.essence: Non-communicable chronic diseases (cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic lung disease, cancer, chronic kidney disease, depression) cause about three-quarters of deaths worldwide (2019) and most of the work of health systems, yet almost all of their management happens outside any clinic: in the patient's decisions about food, activity, smoking, tablets and when to seek help.

nodes.title: Rehabilitation and disability
nodes.essence: Rehabilitation is the part of medicine that works on what a person can do rather than on what disease they have.

nodes.title: Sports, occupational and lifestyle medicine
nodes.essence: Three young specialties share one premise: that what a person does, where they work and how they live are exposures with dose–response relationships to disease, and that changing them is a treatment.

nodes.title: How the specialties interact
nodes.essence: Layers 12, 13 and 14 present the specialties as a tree, but the specialties are a graph: a patient with diabetes is seen by primary care, endocrinology, ophthalmology, nephrology, vascular surgery, cardiology and podiatry, and the quality of their care depends less on any one node than on the edges between them.

nodes.title: Medicine in Society
nodes.essence: Every layer below this one asks how the body works, how it fails, and how a clinician can recognise and reverse the failure. This layer asks what happens when that knowledge meets money, law, values, information systems, inequality, the planet and its own past.

nodes.title: Health Systems
nodes.essence: A clinician never treats a patient in a vacuum. Someone pays, someone decided the treatment was worth paying for, someone designed the ward and the drug chart so that the right dose reaches the right vein, and someone built the record that carried the test result.

nodes.title: Organisation and Financing of Health Systems
nodes.essence: Illness is unpredictable, expensive and concentrated: a small fraction of people account for most spending in any year, and almost nobody can pay for a cancer or an intensive-care stay out of income.

nodes.title: Health Economics and Priority Setting
nodes.essence: A health budget is finite and the things it could buy are not, so funding one treatment is a decision not to fund another. Health economics is decision analysis with that constraint explicit: how much health does a spend buy, compared with what the same money would buy elsewhere?

nodes.title: Patient Safety and Quality Improvement
nodes.essence: Healthcare injures a sizeable minority of the people it treats, mostly not through bad doctors but through ordinary people working in systems that make error easy and recovery hard.

nodes.title: Health Informatics and Artificial Intelligence
nodes.essence: Medicine runs on information: a history, a result, an image, a drug chart, a referral. Health informatics represents that information so it can be stored, moved, found and acted on without losing meaning; the Electronic Health Record (EHR) is its central artefact.

nodes.title: Ethics, Law and the Profession
nodes.essence: Medicine gives one person licensed power over another's body, information and future, exercised when that other is frightened, ill and ignorant of what the first knows.

nodes.title: Medical Ethics
nodes.essence: Medical ethics decides what ought to be done when medicine's power meets a particular person, and gives reasons others can examine.

nodes.title: Consent, Capacity and Confidentiality
nodes.essence: Touching a person without agreement is a battery, and repeating what they told you in confidence is a breach of trust; medicine does both daily and is lawful only because of consent and a confidentiality rule with defined exceptions.

nodes.title: Professionalism, Regulation and Medical Education
nodes.essence: A profession is an occupation society allows to control its own entry, standards and discipline in exchange for a promise to put the public's interest first.

nodes.title: Populations and the Future
nodes.essence: The rest of the tree explains disease in one body and its treatment in one consultation.

nodes.title: Social Determinants and Health Inequity
nodes.essence: In every society with data, health follows social position step by step: each rung down in income, education or occupation brings shorter life and more disease, with no threshold below which the effect stops and no ceiling above which it ends.

nodes.title: Global Health and Pandemics
nodes.essence: Global health is the social gradient drawn between countries instead of within one, plus the fact that microbes do not carry passports. A child born in sub-Saharan Africa in the early 2020s had roughly a 7% chance of dying before age five; one born in Western Europe, about 0.4%.

nodes.title: Environmental and Planetary Health
nodes.essence: The body is an open system that takes in air, water, food and heat from its surroundings, so the state of those surroundings is a medical variable.

nodes.title: History of Medicine
nodes.essence: Medicine's history is not a list of discoveries but a sequence of frames, each a theory of what disease is and therefore of where to look for it, and each displaced when it could no longer explain what a new instrument or a new kind of counting revealed.

nodes.title: The Future of Medicine
nodes.essence: Predicting medicine's future has a poor record: the end of infectious disease was announced in the 1960s, gene therapy was a decade away in 1990, and the genome was to deliver personalised medicine by 2010.
